Crew members can record sleep, mood, fatigue, body discomfort, and optional vital signs. Drawing on NASA and Canadian Space Agency resources, it provides source-linked explanations of how measurements are taken, why they matter, and when to seek medical support. It stores records locally, reducing reliance on remote services for everyday tracking. As a decision-support prototype, it helps crews recognize changes and communicate concerns while keeping mission medical checklists and flight surgeons central to care.
details:
ASTRA is a visual health-monitoring and decision-support web application designed to help astronauts track their wellbeing, understand changes, and find guidance during a medical emergency. It addresses the challenge of making health information accessible to crew members who may be far from Earth and unable to receive immediate specialist support.

The application brings together daily check-ins, a health dashboard, an interactive body map, historical records, measurement reminders, and an emergency guidance flow. Astronauts can record sleep duration and quality, fatigue, mood, stress, team cohesion, dizziness, vision symptoms, and body discomfort. Optional fields support readings from appropriate equipment, including heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, temperature, and blood glucose. Expandable help explains how measurements are recorded, why they matter, and where the supporting information comes from.

ASTRA compares the latest reading with the seven preceding entries to highlight changes from the individual’s baseline. Its numerical rules are explicitly labelled as prototype rules rather than medical thresholds. When information is missing or there is insufficient history, the application displays “Not assessed.” Charts show recorded values over time, while colour, icons, and text help users interpret status without relying on colour alone. The body map provides another way to explore this information by selecting a region such as the head, chest, back, arms, or legs.

The project’s creativity lies in connecting these features into one understandable workflow: record an observation, explore its context, review changes, and find an appropriate next step. The anatomy-centred interface makes health information approachable, while source-linked explanations connect the visual experience to research. A muted ISS/Earth video introduces the application, with playback controls and a still-image alternative for reduced-motion preferences.

We developed ASTRA using TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, and react-body-map. Git and GitHub supported collaboration and version control. Crew profiles and health records are stored locally using browser storage; the prototype requires no backend or custom hardware. Device measurements are entered manually, and direct sensor integration remains future work.

Our team considered NASA’s five spaceflight hazards, drawing on NASA and Canadian Space Agency resources alongside published research. We also considered accessibility, connectivity, missing data, and the limits of self-assessment. The interface supports larger text, light and dark themes, responsive layouts, and keyboard-accessible controls. Radiation exposure requires dosimetry, and vision symptom reports cannot replace specialist examinations for spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome. Emergency mode supports access to guidance and mission procedures; ASTRA does not provide a medical diagnosis or replace trained medical personnel.

The intended benefit is a clearer, more consistent way for crews to organize observations and communicate health concerns. Records remain available locally, and an already-loaded application can operate without remote API calls; fresh offline loading is a future improvement. We verified functionality through 29 automated tests, a production build, and browser checks covering authentication, record handling, navigation, themes, and mobile layouts.

Future development would include medical-specialist review, approved device integration, and verified configurations for spacecraft and lunar habitats. The same accessible, locally stored approach could also be explored for remote communities on Earth, subject to appropriate adaptation and validation.
